question.text: An equal-weighted custom index (base 100) has 5 constituents with 1-day returns: Stock P +30%, Stock Q -10%, Stock R +15%, Stock S +0%, Stock T +25%. Ms. Kavita Bhatia, benchmark analyst at Ganga Capital AIF, must compute the 1-day index value using the arithmetic-mean methodology described in Chapter 10. What is the new index level?

answer.text: 121.0 — based on weighted-average of gains net of losses.
112.0 — based on simple arithmetic mean of constituent returns.
126.0 — based on geometric mean of constituent returns.
115.0 — based on market-cap weighted return of the five stocks.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 10.3.3 (Illustration 10.6), an equal-weighted index moves based on the arithmetic mean of percentage returns. Mean = (30 + (-10) + 15 + 0 + 25) / 5 = 60/5 = 12%. New index = 100 * (1 + 0.12) = 112.0. The Trap: Option A omits the division by 5. Option C applies geometric mean which some equal-weighted indices do use, but the Chapter's primary formula is arithmetic. Option D is the value-weighted computation, not equal-weighted. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM) distinguishes arithmetic vs geometric (time-weighted) returns for performance reporting. XV (Research Analyst) tests index return methodology. Manager's Pro-Tip: Equal-weighted indices force periodic rebalancing — if you benchmark your Cat III small-cap AIF to NIFTY Small Cap 250 Equal-Weight, model the incremental transaction cost drag before committing in the PPM. LPs ask 'why did you beat/lag the benchmark by 80 bps?' and rebalancing friction is a frequent hidden reason.
